title: History Made in Michigan: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed Wins Heated Senate Race
snippet: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan's high-stakes U.S. Senate race, becoming the nation's first Muslim senator amidst a Democratic midterm sweep.
content:
DETROIT — In a landmark victory that reshapes the political landscape, progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan's fiercely contested U.S. Senate race, officially becoming the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican candidate Mike Rogers to claim the seat left vacant by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The victory capped off a decisive night for Democrats, who reclaimed control of both the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives in a 2026 midterm wave.

Addressing an ecstatic crowd of supporters in Detroit, El-Sayed reflected on his unlikely trajectory. "You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates," he told the room. "Thank you. This is all yours."

A Victory Sealed Through Interparty Turbulence

The hard-fought victory came despite a chaotic final week marked by intraparty drama. Just days before the election, Rep. Haley Stevens—the moderate Democrat whom El-Sayed narrowly defeated in the August primary—shattered party unity by crossing party lines to endorse Rogers, a 63-year-old former congressman.

The rift escalated over an outside progressive group's controversial advertisement linking U.S. military support for Israel to rising domestic grocery prices. When Stevens called on El-Sayed to explicitly denounce the ad, his campaign asked her to stay away from a planned unity appearance. Stevens subsequently announced her support for Rogers, telling reporters the choice was a "weight off my shoulders."

The betrayal sparked immediate backlash from Democratic leadership. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel declared that Stevens was no longer a member of the state party, while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer publicly slammed her reversal as a "despicable betrayal."

Fending Off High-Profile Republican Attacks

Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed faced persistent attacks from top Republicans targeting his faith and background. Former President Donald Trump called him a "jihadist," Vice President JD Vance claimed he had "zero attachment" to the United States, and Rogers made unsubstantiated claims tying him to the Muslim Brotherhood.

El-Sayed, a U.S.-born native of Michigan and the son of Egyptian immigrants, met the attacks head-on with a sharp, pugnacious campaign style. At a rally in Grand Rapids late last month, he pushed back against Trump's taunts directly: "He can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro."

Addressing critics who questioned his faith on the trail, El-Sayed emphasized his commitment to serving all Michiganders. "I'm not running to be a Muslim senator," he said during a recent town hall. "I'm running for the U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim."

From Public Health Official to Capitol Hill

El-Sayed’s ascension marks a major turning point for Michigan politics, where establishment candidates have historically dominated statewide races. A former Rhodes Scholar and medical doctor, El-Sayed previously led the Detroit Health Department and gained national attention during his 2018 gubernatorial bid, which earned endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Running on an unapologetic platform advocating for Medicare for All and major shifts in foreign policy, El-Sayed successfully mobilized young and left-leaning voters disillusioned with traditional politics. His victory proves his core political campaign thesis: that bold, populist progressives can win critical swing states in national elections.
